AWARD WINNING MAGAZINE
(Paoli, PA) Each year the National In
terfraternity Foundation, Inc. sponsors a
contest for articles which have appeared
in fraternity and/or sorority magazines,
articles which deal with the role fraterni
ties play in the advancement of the quali
ty of higher education or are positive re
flections upon or constructive criticism of
the college fraternity system. When Psi
Upsilon entered this contest last year for
the first time, it did so with little hope of
winning, considering that most of the 57
fraternities which were competing had
much larger and more elaborate maga
zines and, thus, were more likely to be
recognized. It was with great surprise and
pride that Psi Upsilon accepted the first
place award last year for an article on
hazing written by Richard D. Dadey, Jr. ,
Pi '80. And now, for the second year in a
row, Psi Upsilon was again honored for its
journalism, this time with the second
place award for an article which appeared
in the Spring, 1984 issue of the DI
AMOND, entitled "Isolated Phe
nomenon or Impending Pandemic?"
Written by Mark D. Bauer, Omega '83,
the article dealt with the recent decisions
to abolish fraternities at Amherst and Col
by Colleges �
the factors which precipi
tated these decisions, their effect on
fraternity systems elsewhere, and the
question of whether this is a localized
problem or a precursor to the end of the
North American college fraternity. The
Fraternity is deply indebted to Mark
Bauer for attaining this honor for Psi Up
silon.
NEO-CONSERVATIVE"
EXPANSION
(Providence, RI; Berkeley, CA; Ithaca,
NY) Every new member of Psi Upsilon
learns that the Fraternity's expansion
policy has always been conservative. Psi
U has added one new chapter every five
years, on the average, but this neglects
the fact that one-half ofour chapters were
founded in the first or last ten years of the
Fraternity! This academic year, however,
the Fraternity's policy toward expansion
may best be described as neo-conservative, for it is hoped that the first steps will
be undertaken to reactivate our Sigma
Chapter at Brown University and our
Epsilon Chapter at the University of Cali
fornia at Berkeley. Furthermore, at its
autumn meeting, the Executive Council
voted to reactivate our Chi Chapter at
Cornell University, where a group known
as the Owl Club has been operating for
the past year in anticipation of a reacti
vated Chi (see article on page 9). By the
time this publication reaches its readers,
the eleven men will have been pledged
and the first plans made for their eventual
initiation!

(Paoli, PA) After a long absence, Psi U
sweetheart pins, miniature replicas of the
Psi Upsilon badge, are now available at a
cost of $11.75 from the Fraternity's offi

In addition, badges, pledge pins, rings,
keys, neckties, bowties, songbooks, flags,
pledge manuals, Sesquicentennial plates,
and initiation equipment are always avail
able through the International office.
Please contact the office at 215-647-4830

THE ANCIENT PYRAMID OF
SCHENECTADY
(Schenectady, NY) Psi Upsilon is not a
"typical" college fraternity and neither
were its gifts to Union College, alma ma
ter of its founders, on the occasions of its
Geological timetable, Psi Upsilon's gift
to Union CoUege on the occasion of its
150th anniversary.
Centennial and Sesquicentennial
anniversaries. In 1933 Psi Upsilon do
nated an enormous base to an even more
enormous flagpole, inscribed with the
names of the seven known founders. Not
to be outdone, the Sesquicentennial Con
vention presented Union College with a
gift older than the College, or the human
race for that matter �
a geological time
table in the shape ofa pyramid. Originally
constructed in 1934, the pyramid had de
teriorated and fallen prey to vandals in its
remote location. At Union's request, Psi
Upsilon undertook the project of relocat
ing and restoring the pyramid as its gift to
Union College. Unfortunately construc
tion had only begun last year, so partici
pants saw nothing but a cleared site and
an artist's rendering. The monument has
now been completed and is the talk of the
campus. The base and core of the pyra
mid are concrete; its facade is fourteen
layers of rock representing twelve great
eras of geologic time. The structure is ten
feet square and ten feet high.
UAB SETS GOALS
(Paoli, PA) Congratulations to the 198485 members of the Undergraduate Advi
sory Board: Taylor Briggs, lota '85,
Chairman; Gary Pan, Eta '86, Vice
Chairman; Gordon Ferguson, Psi '85; Jim
Schacht, Beta Beta '85; John Stipec, Zeta
Zeta '85; Iain Taylor, Epsilon Phi '85;
Barry Waterman, Omega '85; Richard
Yates, Upsilon '87; and Joe Zaren, Chi
Delta '87. The nine members, elected by
the Convention, serve as an advisory
group to the Executive Council and meet
at the International office in Paoli twice
each year. The Chairman and Vice Chair
man are voting members ofthe Executive
Council. The UAB held its first meeting
in Paoli the weekend of October 19-21.
After a thorough briefing and a Class "A"
tour of Psi U's facilities, they settled in to
discuss the pertinent issues facing the
Fraternity, particularly those which
affect undergraduates. Concrete solu
tions and/or statements were formulated
and a comprehensive report was deliv
ered to the Executive Council at its
November meeting.

141st Convention Commemorates
100th Anniversary of Eta Chapter
What was the 141st Psi Upsilon Inter
national Convention? Was it a celebra
tion, a series of educational workshops,
the annual meeting of Psi Upsilon's leg
islative body, the formation of new
friendships, the commemoration of the
100th anniversary of our Eta Chapter at
Lehigh University, or was the Conven
tion just a lot offun? Based on evaluations
returned from the almost two hundred
Convention participants who traveled to
Bethlehem from the four corners of North
America, the Convention was all of the
above �
and a whole lot more.
Much thought goes into selecting the
site of Psi Upsilon Conventions. A fre
quent consideration is whether a Con
vention can prompt a Chapter into
reaching for greater heights of excel
lence. In the case of the Eta, the Chapter
was happily granted permission to host
the Convention in recognition of and as
the culmination of the Eta's strides to
ward excellence in anticipation of its
100th anniversary.
As any participant could easily tell, a
Psi Upsilon Convention is not planned
overnight. But this Convention was very
special for its planning began several
years ago. Many fraternities suffered
from the extremism frequently found on
college campuses in the late 60's and early
70's. Our Eta Chapter was no exception.
But the Goodale Literary Association
(better known as the GLA �
the Eta's
alumni association) took steps to stem the
decline and to rebuild the Eta, both spir
itually and physically. In 1978 the mag
nificent porch of the Eta was renovated,
thanks to alumni assistance. This was a
physical manifestation of the steps the
Eta was taking to re-establish its promi
nent place among the many Lehigh
fraternities. Under the guidance of the
GLA, especially John Diederich '73, cur
rent president, and Walt "Super" Sieglen
'69, past president, all facets of the Eta
began to sparkle once again. The 141st
Convention was an integral part of the
rejuvenation of the Eta; it served as a sort
of "Coming Out BaU.
"
Frequent planning sessions attended
by the Fraternity's professional staff and
the Eta's Convention Committee began
last April so that by the time delegates
began arriving on Tuesday, August 21,
everything from tickets to transportation
was flowing smoothly. Delegates were
greeted by blue skies, a beautifully
appointed Chapter house, and the dy
namic duo at the registration table �
Kathy McGlone, Lambda '82H, Adminis
trative Director, and Helena McGuin
ness, Financial Secretary. Helena had
the difficult job of staffing the registration
and information table throughout the five
days �
a task often made more compli
cated by the "fun-loving" Eta's. Helena
will long remember sharing her seat with
a pet snake.
Once settled at (air conditioned!) Brod
head House dormitory and nourished at
the University Center dining room, the
delegates gathered at the Eta for an
orientation meeting, conducted by Hen
ry Poor, Gamma '39, Executive Vice
President. In addition to briefing both
rookies and veterans on what to expect
fi-om the Convention, the delegates were
introduced to Ken Ball, Eta '82, Alumni
Convention Chairman, and Chip
Braulick, Eta '84, and David Turner, Eta
'85, Undergraduate Convention CoChairmen. These three gentlemen
worked tirelessly to insure the success of
this Convention, and they deserve and
have our heartfelt thanks.
Divisional Conferences followed the
orientation. These four meetings,
attended by delegates from neighboring
Chapters, afforded a unique opportunity
for undergraduates to discuss common
concerns and to obtain a greater familiar
ity with Psi Upsilon as it exists outside of
one's own Chapter. The Conferences
were moderated by Pierre Barcik, Nu
'84, and Mark Bauer, Omega '83, current
Field Directors; and Vic Gainor, Delta
'83, and Alan Greenspan, Gamma '84,
former undergraduate members of the
Executive Council. During these Confer
ences the Psi Upsilon biennial surveys,
dealing with traditions, drug abuse, haz
ing, and internal operations, were dis
tributed. The results will be discussed
this winter at the Divisional Conferences
and Leadership Seminars.
During the Divisional Conferences the
Executive Committee met to brainstorm
in anticipation ofthe next day's Executive
Council meeting. The open house held
that night and each succeeding night
proved ideal for informal socializing and
exchanging new ideas. Furthermore, the
undergraduate Eta's, always perfect
hosts, took this opportunity to introduce
all the delegates to a Bethlehem delicacy
called "Greekers" �
a hot dog featuring a
peculiar assortment of condiments. Sur
prisingly, the Convention ended without
a single case of food poisoning!
An expanded series of Leadership
Seminars and Educational Workshops,
held on Wednesday, Thursday, and Fri
day, allowed delegates to be exposed to a
wide variety oftopics. Each seminar drew
upon the talents of our alumni: Bill King,
Omicron '73 (Alumni Relations and
Chapter Publications); Bob Corell, Epsi
lon Iota '82 (Chapter Retreat Planning);
Pierre Barcik, Nu '84 (New Member
Education and Scholarship and Lead
ership Development); Mark Bauer,
Omega '83 (Membership Recruitment
and Ritual Enhancement); Andy Ker
stein, Delta '76 (Chapter Finances and
Tax Laws); Jim Heerin, Tau '58 (Legal
Liabihties); and Henry Poor, Gamma '39
(Workship for Alumni).
To be asked to chair one of the six
standing committees that undertake each
convention's legislative concerns is both a
great honor and an enormous responsibil
ity. Each committee chair was asked to
arrive one day early for a thorough brief
ing on the concerns of their committee,
and each performed admirably. Those
selected for the honor this year were:
Vince Darland, Epsilon Omega '85
(Budget and Development); Zbish Pietr
zak, Chi Delta '86 (Chapter Status); Brad
Fresia, Theta Theta '85 (New Business);
Bob Carter, Zeta Tau '85 (Unfinished
Business); Teresa Grocela, Epsilon Iota
'85 (Credentials and Permanent Organi
zation); and Iain Taylor, Epsilon Phi '85
(Nominations).
Some of the most important legislation
passed by the 141st Convention included
the following:

Fraternity office for two weekends each
year to discuss current undergraduate
concerns. The Chairman and Vice
Chairman of the UAB will also serve as
undergraduate members of the Execu

Dr. Peter Likins, President of Lehigh
University, officially welcomed Psi Up
silon to the "hill" (as any delegate can tell
you, it's actually a steep mountain!) at
Wednesday's opening luncheon. Dr.
Likins gave an interesting talk on
Lehigh's outstanding commitment to its
fraternities and how fraternities can and
do aid higher education. After his speech,
the GLA officially announced its 100th
anniversary gift to Lehigh �
a large cam
pus map to be built at the new entrance to
the University.
The 141st Convention was
officially
called to order at 2:00 p.m. on Wednes
day by John Diederich, Eta '73. Russ
McShane, Delta '32, was installed as
Convention President and chaired each
subsequent general meeting.
After its success at the Sesquicenten
nial Convention, it seemed logical to con
tinue the practice of holding a Memorial
Service to honor the generations of de
ceased Psi U's, particularly those who had
passed away in the preceding year. Un
fortunately, what was not anticipated was
the unavoidable, last minute absence of
the brother who planned to lead the ser
vice. Fortunately, the ever- versatile
Henry Poor, with the able assistance of
John Menzies, Pi '41; Bob Morey, Pi '20;
and Russ McShane, Delta '32, guided this
fine tradition through its second year.
Most moving of all were the spontaneous
eulogies delivered by members of the
congregation for brothers they had
known and loved.
After the Memorial Service, it was time
for a practical joke ^
practical in that it
provided a useful lesson; joke in that it
was abit ofa hoax. The schedule called for
a
reception hosted by the UAB featuring
strawberry daiquiris. But, known only to
the Paoli staff, Mrs. Mary Poor, and the
UAB, was the fact that these daquiris con
tained no alcohol, only artificial rum fla
voring. It is impossible to judge the re
sults; many claimed they were never
fooled, while others seemed slightly tip
sy. But, mostimportant of aU, a valuable
lesson was learned �
one does not need
alcohol to enjoy oneselfl
The reception provided a lead-in for
the main event of the evening, a dynamic
talk by Dr. Thomas Goodale, Vice ChanceUor of Student Affairs of the University
of Denver. His presentation, entitled "A
New Look at the Old Sauce," addressed
alcohol abuse and misuse. Dr, Goodale
who was able to speak at the Convention
through a grant from the Psi Upsilon
Foundation, made it clear from the start
that he was a social drinker. What he
wished to discuss was misuse ofalcohol�
the subtle ways in which fraternities often
encourage its misuse and what each of us
can do about it. During the open house
which followed, Mr. Goodale joined the
delegates to continue discussion infor
mally. Many undergraduates left with
advice from Dr. Goodale on how to deal
with specific problems and, probably
even more important, a new
perspective
on the dangers ofalcohol. One Director of
the Foundation said that "bringing Dr.
Goodale to the Convention was one ofthe
best expenditures we've ever made."
Hopefiilly Dr. Goodale's words will be
remembered for a long time to come.
Thursday morning was perhaps the
only frightening moment of the Conven
tion �
it was raining. While no one could
feel glee over Bethlehem Steel's financial
problems, the lack ofthe usual smoke and
Mother Nature's prior charity had made
each day a joy. But rain �
on the day of
the Convention photograph and special
outing! The 7:00 a.m. ConventiOii "Com
mittee meeting that day was more like a
prayer session. By some miracle the skies
cleared just before a decision was made tp
reschedule the photographer.
Thursday evening promised to be
memorable and it certainly was, though
not necessarily for all the proper reasons.
The schedule called for a scenic bus ride
to New Hope, Pennsylvania, where an
authentic steam locomotive waited to car
ry the attendees and a hired caterer eight
miles dovra the track and back. No one
expected the buses to get lost on the way,
and the Convention Committee had no
way of knowing that the train had no
lights on board. But good Psi U's know
how to enjoy themselves, even under the
most trying of circumstances. The long
bus rides gave everyone a chance to ex
pand their repertoire of Psi U songs. Rid
ing and eating in a dark, hundred-yearold train certainly gave everyone some
thing to joke about. AU in aU, and perhaps
in spite of itseff, the special outing turned
out to be a
very enjoyable evening!
At luncheon on Friday we were sched
uled to hear a talk by David C. Amidon,
Jr. , Professor of Urban Studies at Lehigh.
But "talk" does not adequately describe
the event; in actuahty the attendees were
entertained by Professor Amidon.
Addressing a great variety ofpohtical and
social issues, some felt Professor Amidon
managed to shock everyone in the room,
while others were
simply amused. Judg
ing from the lively discussion after the
Professor's speech, at least Psi U cannot

On Friday evening the Convention ad
journed to spectacular Rathbone Hall for
the Executive Council-sponsored cock
tail party and, following that, the high
light of the action-packed five days, the
Convention banquet. Rathbone Hall fea
tures enormous
floor-to-ceiling windows
offering a view of most of the Lehigh Val
ley. Again Mother Nature honored us
and, for the remaining daylight hours, the
banquet attendees enjoyed a splendid
view in addition to fine fellowship.
Camaraderie and brotherhood were in
abundant evidence on this special night.
After singing the "Psi U Doxology," a
beautiful invocation was delivered by
Henry Poor, Gamma '39, for Bob Morey,
Pi '20, who had to leave early. Toasts to
the President ofthe United States and the
Queen of the British Commonwealth and
Canada were offered by Guy Worrell, Eta
'43, and Jim Morton, Epsilon Phi '43,
respectively. Many of the favorite Psi U
songs were sung with great enthusiasm
throughout the evening.
Master of Ceremonies Ken Ball, Eta
'82, lent a capable hand to the occasion.
Featured speakers included Jeff Weber,
Eta '84, undergraduate president at the
time; John Diederich, Eta '73, president
of the Goodale Literary Association; and
Jim Harper, Epsilon Omega '54, Director
of Community Relations at Lehigh. Each
speaker's eloquent remarks were fol
lowed by thunderous applause. It was an
evening to be long remembered, especiaUy the enormously popular open house
that followed.
Special thanks must go to the unbeliev
ably organized and effective Eta Conven
tion Committee: Ken Ball '82, Jim
Creedon '83, John Diederich '73, Perry
Blazewicz '79, Jim Couch '68, Sam Dugan
'71, John Center '69, Don Grunwald '82,
Jim Harper, Epsilon Omega '54, Don
McAUister '70 (also Epsilon Omega '71),
Alex Moeller '78, Steve Moore '84, John
Schneider '78, Walt Sieglen '69, Jim
Swain '83, and Mike Torongo '81.
The undergraduate members of the
Committee deserve more than just a spe
cial commendation. By any standards,
the 141st Convention was flawless. The
Eta demonstrated its commitment to Psi
Upsilon by making the months and years
of preparation for this Convention ob
vious in its execution. They have truly set
the standard for future Conventions.
Even the behind the scenes work �
cleaning up after open houses, shuttling
participants to and from the airport, run
ning errands, etc. �
was truly outstand
ing. Special thanks are extended to: Chip
Braulick '84, David Turner '85, John Hoskins '86, Jeff Weber '84, Bob Dunn '85,
Walter Deichmann '85, Stan Galczynski
'84, Phil Gauffreau '84, Terry Gray '86,
Mike Pagan '85, John Treichler '86, and
Tim Tritsch '85.
The 141st Convention would not have
been a success without the unfailing
cooperation and understanding of Lehigh
University and its Office of Special
Events. Special thanks must also go to
Beverly Couch for organizing the
spouses' program, to Psi U's numerous
roving photographers, and to Mother Na
ture and Bethlehem Steel for clear, blue
skies.
Saturday morning found delegates
saying goodbye, exchanging phone num
bers, and planning roadtrips before de
parting by car, bus, train, or plane.
Though weary, the participants all wore a
smile. The regretful fareweUs attested to
the importance of the Convention as a
sharing experience.
In his welcome letter to delegates. Ken
Ball, Eta '82, said: "There is no greater
way to learn of Psi U �
to learn of
brotherhood �
than to experience it at a
convention. Whether this is your first or
your fifty-first, we hope that the activities
planned and the fraternal interaction that
ensues will kindle in us all a renewed
fervor in Psi Upsilon."
See you August 28-31, 1985 at the Uni
versity of Illinois!

C. Stuart Maurer
Phi '82
C. Stuart Maurer, Phi '82, has joined
the staff of D'Arcy McManus Masius in
St. Louis as an Anheuser-Busch, Inc. re
gional account executive. He is responsi
ble for market planning and media place
ment ofadvertising for the seven Anheus
er-Busch, Inc. beer brands.
Brother Maurer previously was an
account executive with Kenyon & Eckhardt in Detroit. He earned a bachelor's
degree in English from the University of
Michigan in Ann Arbor.
Stephen F. Keller, Epsilon '59, a part
ner in the Los Angeles law firm of LiUick
McHose & Charles, has been elected a
trustee of the Northwestern Mutual Life
Insurance Company in Milwaukee.
Brother Keller was born in Los Angeles
and received his B.S. degree in business
administration from the University of
California at Berkeley in 1959. Three
years later he was awarded a law degree
from the same institution.
Brother Keller is a member of the
board of directors of the Dai-Ichi Kangyo
Bank of California in Los Angeles and of
Clayton Industries in El Monte. He is an
underwriting member of Lloyd's of Lon
don and serves on the board of trustees of
the University of California Berkeley
Foundation and Orthopaedic Hospital.
Brother Keller's election to Northwest
ern Mutual's board of trustees comes af
ter his having served on its Examining
Committee of Policyowners in 1981 and
as its committee chairman in 1982.
James D. Morrissey, Pi '58, a cardiac
surgeon from Stockton, California,
headed a thirteen-member team that
attempted to climb the East Face (on the
border between Tibet and Nepal) of
Mount Everest late last year. Dr. Morris

The East Face, the last unascended face
of Everest, had been chmbed. The next
day three more would retrace their steps
to the summit while four more awaited
their chance. Their chance never came as
high winds and heavy snow drove us off
the mountain."

to the Fraternity office and is on

Owl Club Equals Chi Chapter
Hope or Reality?
when the Chi Chapter was declared
inactive in 1982, it was everyone's hope
that this proud and distinguished Chap
ter might regain its rightful place on Cor
nell's campus just as quickly as possible .
The first step toward achieving this goal
was initiated last year with the formation
of the Owl Club, a group of ten Cornell
freshmen and one sophomore transfer
studentfrom Union College and the The
ta Chapter.
The Owl Club wishes to keep the
Fraternity-at-large abreast of its prog
ress and hereioith presents the following
report:
We the Owl Club have established
ourselves in the Collegetown area of Cor
nell University and hope to soon reacti
vate the Chi Chapter of Psi Upsilon.
The Owl Club is living under one roof
for the first time. Although the size of our
house at 127 Dryden Road is modest for a
fraternity, we have found it adequate for
our needs. Our refurbishing efforts began
with cleaning and painting the interior of
the house, but the finishing touch was
provided with the hanging of composites
and memorabilia from the Chapter house
on 2 Forest Park Lane, which we hope to
re-occupy once formal reactivation has
occurred and our numbers have grown.
Retrieval and restoring of neglected
photos and plaques also helped to height
en our knowledge of the history of our
Chapter. We extend thanks to Chris Hart
'72, Chi alumni president, for his gener
ous donation of personal Psi U memora
bilia.
Many Chi alumni attending Chris
Hart's wedding during the weekend of
September 14 also found time to visit the
newly formed Owl Club. On the eve of
the wedding we hosted a reception for
alumni and University officials. Henry
Poor, Gamma '39, and Alva Tompkins,
Chi '24, helped put meaning behind the
names and faces in the composites. John
Ciavacco, Theta '87, and Bryan McGuirk,
Theta '85, drove over from Union for the
reception on Friday evening. Alva was
our guest throughout the weekend, as
was the new Field Director, Pierre Bar
cik, Nu '84. At the reception and wedding
we met a number of alumni who gracious
ly offered us their support and good
wishes.
Pierre was here for five days getting
acquainted with the Owls. We greatly
appreciated his advice and guidance on
policy and proper conduct for our group.
He spoke in depth with each of the Owl
brothers about the Fraternity, the Chap
ter, and the duties and responsibilities of
each of the respective officers. He also
introduced us to an orderly and efficient
meeting format.
Henry Poor, Pierre Barcik, and Colin
Purcell (Owl Club President) met with
Vice President William Gurowitz and
IFC Chairperson Janiece Oblak of the
University to discuss the progress of the
Owl Club. The tone of the meeting was
optimistic, and we were assured the sup
port of the administration.
Every Sunday evening two of the Owl
brothers prepare a dinner which pre
cedes our weekly meeting. These meals
are a great means to strengthen our
fraternal bonds and to acquaint ourselves
with prospective rushees. Our meetings
have become more efficient and produc
tive, and the various topics discussed
have become more complex as our knowl
edge of organizing a fraternity has im
proved.
Our social agenda consists of outings
such as camping retreats and sailing days,
trips to other Chapters (the Theta and
soon the Pi), and receptions involving the
alumni, such as Homecoming weekend.
Activities such as these help us to grow
closer to one another so that we may build
a strong Chapter with pride and fel
lowship.
Our rush program does not seek to
compete with that of the established
fraternities on campus; we simply do riot
have the capabilities. Our program's
strategy is to appraise potential members
of the Owl Club on a one-to-one basis.
This selection process is actually more
personalized than the pledging system
used by other fraternities. The club's
small size allows us to require that all the
Owls know all rushees. This encourages
us to distinguish between true friendship
and mere acquaintance.
We realize that our first duty is to the
University, which should be true of any
Chapter. First of all we are CorneUians
and then brothers of the Owl Club. We
further realize that the Owl Club is a
positive contribution to the Cornell com
munity. Our contribution lies in offering
an alternative to the fraternities now ou
campus and a unique opportunity to build
the foundations ofa strong brotherhood.
The initial steps in re-establishing the Chi
Chapter of Psi Upsilon at Cornell Uni
versity have been made. We also under
stand that the challenging steps involved
in restoring the former stature of the Chi
have yet to be taken.

ing, the Executive Council officially
reactivated the Chi Chapter at Cornell
